lessons.body:
HTML Foundations

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the skeleton of every web page. It is not a programming language — it is a markup language: you write tags that tell the browser what each piece of content is. A heading is <h1>, a paragraph is <p>, a link is <a> and an image is <img>. Most tags come in pairs — an opening tag and a closing tag — and the content sits between them.

Every page starts with the same bones: <!DOCTYPE html>, then <html> containing a <head> (title, metadata, links to CSS) and a <body> (everything the visitor sees). Links use the href attribute for their destination, and images use src for the file plus alt text that describes the picture when it cannot load.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head><title>My first page</title></head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>
    <p>This is my first web page.</p>
    <a href="https://example.com">Visit Example</a>
  </body>
</html>

Step by step: the browser reads the tags top to bottom and builds the page. <h1> renders the biggest heading; <p> renders a paragraph; <a href="..."> renders a clickable link. If a tag is misspelled the browser does its best anyway — so always check your page in the browser as you write it.

mcqs.q: What does HTML stand for?
mcqs.why: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language — it marks up content with tags so the browser knows what each part is.

mcqs.q: Which tag creates the largest heading on a page?
mcqs.why: <h1> is the largest heading; <h2> to <h6> get progressively smaller. <head> is metadata, not a visible heading.

mcqs.q: Which tag is used for a paragraph of text?
mcqs.why:
Paragraphs use

. The other three are not real HTML tags.

mcqs.q: Which attribute sets where a link goes when clicked?
mcqs.why: The href attribute holds the link destination, e.g. <a href="https://example.com">. src is for images and scripts.

mcqs.q: Which tag embeds an image in a page?
mcqs.why: Images use the self-closing tag with a src attribute, e.g. .

lessons.body:
CSS Styling & Layouts

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how a page looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. A CSS rule has a selector (which elements it targets) and a declaration block of property-value pairs. p { color: blue; } makes every paragraph blue. A class selector starts with a dot (.card targets class="card"), and an id selector starts with a hash (#header targets id="header").

The box model is the key idea: every element is a box made of content, then padding (space inside the border), then the border, then margin (space outside the border). padding pushes content away from the element's own edge; margin pushes other elements away. Getting these two mixed up is the most common beginner layout bug.

.card {
  background: white;
  padding: 16px;
  margin: 12px;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;
}

Step by step: the browser applies every matching rule, and when two rules clash the more specific selector wins. An external stylesheet is linked from the <head> with <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">, so one CSS file can style the whole site.

mcqs.q: Which CSS property changes the colour of text?
mcqs.why: The color property sets text colour. background sets the background colour; there is no text-color property.

mcqs.q: How do you select every element with class="card" in CSS?
mcqs.why: Class selectors start with a dot: .card. A hash (#card) selects an id, and a bare word selects a tag name.

mcqs.q: What does the CSS box model include, from the inside out?
mcqs.why: Inside out it is content, then padding, then border, then margin.

mcqs.q: Which property adds space INSIDE an element's border, around its content?
mcqs.why: padding is the space inside the border. margin is the space outside the border.

mcqs.q: Where does the <link> tag for an external stylesheet belong?
mcqs.why: Stylesheets are linked in the <head>, so the browser loads the styles before it renders the page body.

tasks.answer: CSS uses the American spelling color, not colour. The browser ignores unknown property names, so nothing changed.
tasks.hint: Check the spelling of the property name — CSS uses American English.
tasks.prompt: This CSS does nothing. Fix it so the heading turns red.
tasks.title: Fix the broken rule

lessons.title: CSS Styling & Layouts

lessons.body:
Responsive Design with Flexbox & Grid

A responsive page adapts to any screen — phone, tablet or desktop. The starting point is the viewport meta tag, <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">, which tells a phone browser that the page width equals the device width instead of pretending to be a wide desktop page. After that, @media queries apply different styles at different widths, for example stacking columns vertically below 600px.

Two layout systems do the heavy lifting. Flexbox (display: flex) lines items up in a row or column: justify-content spaces them along the main axis and align-items along the other axis. Grid (display: grid) lays items out in rows and columns, e.g. grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr makes two equal columns. Use flexbox for one-dimensional rows; use grid for two-dimensional page layouts.

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .row { flex-direction: column; }
}
.row { display: flex; gap: 16px; }
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }

Step by step: build the mobile layout first, then add media queries that widen it for larger screens. Test by shrinking the browser window — if anything overflows sideways, a fixed width somewhere is the culprit.

mcqs.q: Which CSS rule applies styles only when the screen is 600px wide or less?
mcqs.why: Media queries use @media (max-width: 600px) { ... }. The other forms are not valid CSS.

mcqs.q: Which display value turns an element into a flex container?
mcqs.why: display: flex makes the element a flex container; its children become flex items. flexbox is not a valid display value.

mcqs.q: Which flexbox property centres items along the main (horizontal) axis?
mcqs.why: justify-content works along the main axis (horizontal for a row). align-items works along the cross axis.

options: It tells the browser the page width matches the device width
mcqs.q: What does the viewport meta tag do?
mcqs.why: Without it, phones render the page at desktop width and shrink it; with it, the page width matches the device.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a CSS Grid property?
mcqs.why: grid-template-columns defines grid columns. flex-direction belongs to flexbox, and grid-color does not exist.

tasks.answer: display: flex turns .row into a flex container, so its children line up in a row.
tasks.hint: The value is the name of the layout system itself.
tasks.prompt: Complete the CSS so the container becomes a flex container.
tasks.title: Fill in the blank

lessons.body:
JavaScript Basics

JavaScript makes pages interactive: it reacts to clicks, changes content, and talks to servers. Variables store values — let declares a value you can reassign later, const declares one you cannot, and the old var is best avoided. Values have types: "hello" is a string, 42 is a number, true is a boolean, and [1, 2, 3] is an array.

Two things trip up beginners. First, == compares loosely ("5" == 5 is true) while === compares strictly ("5" === 5 is false) — always use ===. Second, functions package reusable behaviour: function greet(name) { return "Hello, " + name; } can be called as greet("Sid"). Control flow comes from if/else for decisions and for/while loops for repetition.

let score = 0;
const passMark = 40;
function addPoints(n) { score = score + n; }
addPoints(50);
if (score >= passMark) {
  console.log("Passed!");
} else {
  console.log("Try again.");
}

Step by step: addPoints(50) raises the score to 50, the if checks it against 40, and console.log("Passed!") prints to the browser console (open it with F12). console.log is your best debugging friend — print values whenever the code surprises you.

mcqs.q: Which keyword declares a variable whose value CAN be reassigned later?
mcqs.why: let allows reassignment; const does not. static and final are not JavaScript variable keywords.

options: The two are the same object
mcqs.q: What does === check in JavaScript?
mcqs.why: === is strict equality: both value and type must match. == is loose and converts types first.

mcqs.q: Which statement prints a value to the browser console?
mcqs.why: console.log() writes to the console (F12). print() is Python, echo() is PHP.

mcqs.q: What is the type of the value "42" (with quotes)?
mcqs.why: Quotes make it a string, even though the characters look like a number. Without quotes, 42 is a number.

mcqs.q: Which loop keeps running while its condition stays true?
mcqs.why: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. if runs once; switch picks one branch.

tasks.answer: x starts at 3, then x + 2 is 5, which is stored back into x, so console.log(x) prints 5.
tasks.hint: Work through the lines top to bottom, updating x each time.
tasks.title: Trace the variables

lessons.title: JavaScript Basics

lessons.body:
DOM Manipulation & Events

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live, tree-shaped view of the page: every tag becomes a node you can reach from JavaScript. document.getElementById("title") grabs the element with id="title", and document.querySelector(".card") grabs the first element matching any CSS selector. Once you have an element, textContent changes its text, style.color changes its colour, and classList.add("hidden") toggles a CSS class.

Events make pages respond: button.addEventListener("click", handler) runs handler every time the button is clicked. The handler receives an event object, and inside it event.target is the element that was actually clicked. The golden rule: your script must run after the elements exist — put <script> tags at the end of <body>, or the lookup returns null.

const btn = document.getElementById("likeBtn");
const count = document.getElementById("likeCount");
let likes = 0;
btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
  likes = likes + 1;
  count.textContent = likes + " likes";
});

Step by step: the first two lines grab the button and the counter element. Each click runs the handler, which adds one to likes and writes the new text into the counter — so the number on the page goes up by one every click.

mcqs.q: Which method selects an element by its id attribute?
mcqs.why: getElementById("myId") returns the element with that id. The other method names do not exist.

mcqs.q: Which property changes the text inside an element?
mcqs.why: textContent sets the element's text. value is for form inputs, not for ordinary elements.

mcqs.q: How do you run a function every time a button is clicked?
mcqs.why: addEventListener("click", handler) registers the function. Note: handler() with brackets would call it immediately instead of on click.

mcqs.q: Which method returns the FIRST element matching a CSS selector?
mcqs.why: querySelector() returns the first match; querySelectorAll() returns all matches as a list.

options: Sets the element's text colour to red
mcqs.q: What does element.style.color = "red" do?
mcqs.why: The style object mirrors CSS properties in JavaScript (color becomes style.color), so this sets the text colour.

tasks.answer: Each click adds 1 to likes and rewrites the counter text, so after two clicks likes is 2 and the page shows "2 likes".
tasks.hint: Count the clicks — the handler runs once per click.
tasks.prompt: The button starts with the text "0 likes". What happens after two clicks?
tasks.title: Predict the output

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation & Events

lessons.body:
Build a Portfolio Project

Now combine everything: a one-page portfolio is the classic first project because it proves HTML structure, CSS layout and a little JavaScript in one place. Plan four sections before writing code — a hero (your name + one line about what you do), an about section, a projects grid with three cards, and a contact section with links. Sketch it on paper first; the layout decisions are easier there than in code.

Build mobile-first: single column, then a media query that turns the projects into a grid on wider screens. Add one small JavaScript touch — a mobile menu toggle, a dark-mode switch, or a form that shows a thank-you message. Then test: shrink the window, click every link, and open it on your phone. Finally deploy it free with GitHub Pages so the link can go on your resume.

<header>
  <h1>Siddartha Jamandla</h1>
  <p>B.Tech AI & ML student, building with Python & JavaScript</p>
</header>
<section id="projects">
  <div class="card">...</div>
</section>

Step by step: hero first (it is what visitors see), then about, then projects, then contact. A finished, deployed portfolio beats ten half-finished projects — ship this one, then improve it a little every week.

options: Your name and what you do
A list of every course taken
mcqs.q: What should a portfolio's first (hero) section usually show?
mcqs.why: The hero answers who you are and what you do in one glance. Details like marksheets belong deeper in the page, if anywhere.

mcqs.q: Which file do browsers load first when opening a website folder?
mcqs.why: Web servers treat index.html as the default entry file for a folder.

options: The layout must work on small screens too
mcqs.q: Why should you test your portfolio on a phone as well as a laptop?
mcqs.why: Most visitors will open it on a phone; a layout that only works on desktop looks broken to them.

options: Hosts a static website free from a repository
mcqs.q: What does GitHub Pages do?
mcqs.why: GitHub Pages serves static sites (HTML/CSS/JS) straight from a repo, free — it does not run a backend.

mcqs.q: Which tag links a page to its external CSS file?
mcqs.why: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> in the <head> loads the stylesheet. <style> is for inline CSS, not for linking a file.

tasks.answer: Hero first, then about, projects, contact; single column on mobile, grid on desktop; deploy via GitHub Pages and put the link on your resume.
tasks.expected: A deployed portfolio link with all four sections, working on phone and desktop
tasks.hint: Start with the HTML sections, then the CSS, then one small JavaScript touch.
tasks.prompt: Build a one-page portfolio: hero with your name and one line about what you do, an about section, three project cards, and a contact section. Make it responsive and deploy it on GitHub Pages.
tasks.title: Ship your portfolio
